worked_examples.title: Follow the input
narration: Let f square its input and let g add three. We want f of g of two. The parentheses tell us which machine receives the input first.
Two enters g. Adding three produces five. Keep that five: it is the output of the first machine and the input of the second.
Now five enters f. Squaring gives twenty-five. We have not multiplied the functions. We have passed a value through them in order.
Follow the numbers from left to right in the machine diagram, even though the notation names the outer function first.

worked_examples.title: Replace the entire input
narration: Instead of a particular number, let the input be x. The first machine returns x plus three.
The outer function squares its whole input. Put brackets around x plus three before squaring. Those brackets are doing mathematical work.
If we expand, the result is x squared plus six x plus nine. The middle term comes from the two cross products.
Check with x equal to two: four plus twelve plus nine gives twenty-five, matching our machine calculation. A numerical check connects the symbolic result to the first example.

worked_examples.title: Reverse the machines
narration: Now reverse the order. Square two first, giving four. Add three next, giving seven.
The graphs show the two composite functions. They are different curves because the two instructions act in different orders.
At x equal to two, one curve has height twenty-five and the other has height seven. This single counterexample is enough to show the functions are not equal.
Some pairs of functions do commute, so order does not always change the output. The reliable habit is to calculate both compositions rather than assume.

opening.title: Can you dry a car before washing it?
narration: Would you run a car through the dryer before the soap? The same two machines can produce a different result when you reverse them.
Today we will use that idea to read, calculate, and check composite functions.

hook.title: One output becomes the next input
narration: The car-wash picture is an analogy for order. Soap is one operation and drying is another.
In mathematics, the first function produces a value. The second function receives that value. The functions below use numbers, not cars.

concept.title: Read from the inside outward
narration: In f of g of x, start with x inside the innermost parentheses.
Apply g first. Then carry its complete output into f.
The labels stay in place while the input travels through the machines. Track the hand-off between them.

definition.title: Composition is a hand-off
narration: The composition f composed with g is the function that sends x to f of g of x.
The input must belong to the domain of g, and the result g of x must belong to the domain of f. Without both conditions, the composition is undefined.

formula.title: The inner operation happens first
narration: The small composition circle is not a multiplication sign.
In this example, g adds three and f squares. Keep the whole expression x plus three inside the square.

mistakes.title: Same machines. Wrong order.
narration: A common wrong answer is seven for f of g of two. Seven comes from squaring first and then adding three.
That calculation answers g of f of two instead. Repair the reasoning by naming the inner function before you do any arithmetic.

summary.title: Name the first machine
narration: Composition means use the output of one function as the input of another.
Read from the inside outward, preserve brackets, and check domain restrictions.
One final challenge: can you find two different functions for which reversing the order gives the same result?

student_pause.spoken_prompt: Your turn. Let f of x equal two x minus one, and g of x equal x squared. Find f of g of three. Choose the first function before calculating.
student_pause.spoken_answer: Apply g first: three squared gives nine. Then f of nine is eighteen minus one, which is seventeen.

misconception.correction: Apply g first: g(2)=5, then f(5)=25.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the calculation to an input and output situation

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Let f double its input and subtract one. Let g square its input. Find f of g of three.
solution_narration: The inner function g squares three, producing nine.
Use nine as the input of f. Eighteen minus one is seventeen.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Now f adds four and g multiplies by three. Find g of f of two.
solution_narration: Start with f: two plus four is six.
Then apply g: three times six is eighteen. The named outer function is the second operation.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Let f square its input and let g subtract one. Write a formula for f of g of x.
solution_narration: Replace the input of the squaring function with the whole expression x minus one.
Brackets are required. Expanding gives x squared minus two x plus one, not x squared minus one.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Let f double the input and g add five. Compare both orders at an input of one.
solution_narration: Adding five then doubling gives twelve.
Doubling then adding five gives seven. These functions do not commute.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Let f be the real square-root function and g subtract four. Which real inputs are allowed in f composed with g?
solution_narration: The expression under a real square root must be nonnegative.
Require x minus four to be at least zero. The domain is all x greater than or equal to four.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Finally, f adds two and g adds five. Do these two functions commute? Give a formula that proves your answer.
solution_narration: Both orders add a total of seven.
The formulas agree for every real input, so these two functions do commute. Compare this proof with the earlier single counterexample.

worked_examples.title: Undo the operations
narration: The forward function doubles a number, then adds five. Starting at three produces eleven.
To recover the input from eleven, undo the last operation first. Subtract five, giving six.
Then divide by two, giving three. Reversing the order of the operations is as important as changing them.

worked_examples.title: Solve for the original input
narration: Write y equals two x plus five. Interchange the input and output labels.
Now solve x equals two y plus five for y. Subtract five and divide by two.
The inverse formula is x minus five over two. Its input is an output from the original function.

worked_examples.title: Reflect input and output
narration: Swapping each input and output swaps the coordinates of each graph point.
The point three, eleven becomes eleven, three. Reflection across the line y equals x performs this swap.
A horizontal line must not hit the original graph twice if its inverse is to be a function. A restricted domain can sometimes repair that problem.

opening.title: Can you recover the starting number?
narration: A machine hides a number, doubles it, and adds five. The display says eleven.
Which operation would you undo first?

concept.title: Undo the last step first
narration: An inverse reverses a mapping. If the forward function sends three to eleven, the inverse sends eleven to three.
The word inverse describes the operation, not a reciprocal.

mistakes.title: Inverse is not reciprocal
narration: One over f of x takes a reciprocal. It does not generally recover the original input.
For f of x equal two x plus five, the inverse is x minus five over two. Compare these two formulas carefully.

student_pause.spoken_prompt: Find the inverse of h of x equals three x minus four. Undo the last operation first.
student_pause.spoken_answer: Add four, then divide by three. The inverse is x plus four over three.

misconception.wrong_reasoning: The inverse is one divided by f of x.
misconception.correction: Swap input and output, then solve for the new output.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the calculation to an input and output situation

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Find the inverse of three x minus four.
solution_narration: Undo subtracting four by adding four.
Undo multiplying by three by dividing by three. The inverse is x plus four over three.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Find the inverse of x plus one divided by two.
solution_narration: Reverse the final division first: multiply the output by two.
Then subtract one. Relabelling the input gives the inverse two x minus one.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: For f of x equal to two x plus five, find the inverse evaluated at nine.
solution_narration: Subtract five from nine, then divide by two. You recover two.
Check by applying the original function: two times two plus five returns nine.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Does squaring on all real numbers have an inverse function? Explain.
solution_narration: Both two and negative two map to four.
An inverse would have to send four to two different outputs. Restricting the original domain to nonnegative numbers makes the square-root inverse possible.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Now restrict the original squaring function to nonnegative inputs. Find its inverse and domain.
solution_narration: Choose the nonnegative square root because the original input was nonnegative.
The inverse is square root x, with a nonnegative domain.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Verify by composition that the inverse of four x plus one really undoes the function.
solution_narration: First find the inverse x minus one over four.
Composing produces x minus one plus one, which simplifies to x. This verifies the forward composition for every real input.

worked_examples.title: Mirror symmetry
narration: Inputs with equal magnitudes and opposite signs give the same output.
For example, two and negative two both produce five. The graph reflects onto itself across the vertical axis.
Substituting negative x confirms that the equality holds for every input in the domain, not just the two we checked.

worked_examples.title: A half-turn around the origin
narration: An odd function changes the sign of the output when the input changes sign.
Negative two gives negative ten while positive two gives positive ten.
The graph matches itself after a half-turn around the origin. Algebra proves the relationship for the whole domain.

worked_examples.title: A counterexample is enough
narration: A function can be neither even nor odd. Evaluate this one at one and negative one.
The outputs are two and zero. Zero is neither two nor negative two.
One counterexample rejects each proposed identity. Exponent labels alone are not a substitute for this test.

opening.title: Mirror, half-turn, or neither?
narration: A butterfly suggests mirror symmetry. A pinwheel suggests a half-turn.
Can a function have either symmetry, or neither? Test the input and its opposite.

misconception.wrong_reasoning: An odd power somewhere makes a function odd.
misconception.correction: Test f(-x) against f(x) and -f(x), including its domain.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the calculation to an input and output situation

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Classify x to the fourth plus two as even, odd, or neither.
solution_narration: A negative input raised to the fourth has the same fourth power.
The constant stays unchanged, so f of negative x equals f of x. The function is even.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Classify three x cubed.
solution_narration: Changing x to negative x changes the sign of the cube.
The whole output changes sign, so the function is odd.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Classify x cubed plus one.
solution_narration: At one the output is two, while at negative one it is zero.
The pair fails both identities. Adding a constant to an odd function generally breaks its origin symmetry.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Can the zero function be both even and odd? Test both definitions.
solution_narration: Zero equals its own negative.
The zero function satisfies both equations on its symmetric domain, so it is both even and odd.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Classify one over x on the nonzero real numbers.
solution_narration: The domain contains x and negative x together.
Substitution gives negative one over x, which is the negative of f of x. The function is odd.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: If the domain of x squared is only the nonnegative reals, can you call the function even?
solution_narration: The standard even-function definition requires a domain symmetric about zero.
Two is allowed but negative two is not. The unrestricted formula looks even, but this restricted function does not meet that domain requirement.

worked_examples.title: Move the vertex
narration: The square reaches its minimum when its input is zero. For the shifted expression, x minus two is zero at x equals two.
That is why subtracting two inside the function moves the vertex right, not left.
Adding three outside the function raises every output by three. The new vertex is two, three.

worked_examples.title: Reflect the outputs
narration: The negative sign outside the function changes the sign of every output.
The factor two doubles its magnitude. A height of four becomes negative eight.
The graph therefore reflects across the horizontal axis and stretches vertically by a factor of two.

worked_examples.title: Combine the changes
narration: Set x plus one equal to zero to locate the new vertex horizontally. This gives x equal to negative one.
The outside factor doubles outputs relative to the parabola before the final vertical shift. Subtracting three then lowers the graph.
Track a point as well as the vertex. The point zero, zero on the original becomes negative one, negative three.

opening.title: Why does minus two move a graph right?
narration: The formula subtracts two, yet the graph moves right. That apparent contradiction disappears when you track the input.

misconception.wrong_reasoning: x minus five moves the graph left five.
misconception.correction: The inner input becomes zero at x=5, so it moves right five.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the calculation to an input and output situation

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Find the vertex of one half times x minus five squared, minus one.
solution_narration: The square vanishes at x equal to five.
The remaining output is negative one, giving vertex five, negative one.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Which way does x plus three inside a square shift the parabola?
solution_narration: The original vertex input was zero.
Now the inner input is zero at negative three, so the graph shifts left three.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Describe the vertex and opening direction of negative x squared plus four.
solution_narration: There is no horizontal shift, and adding four moves the vertex to zero, four.
The negative leading coefficient reflects the parabola, so it opens downward.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Where does the original vertex zero, zero move under three times x minus one squared?
solution_narration: It moves right one.
The vertical stretch multiplies a zero height by three, so the vertex height stays zero.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: For an arbitrary function f, what horizontal scale factor does f of two x produce?
solution_narration: An original input a is reached when two x equals a.
The new x coordinate is a over two, so horizontal distances compress by a factor of one half.

practice_set.spoken_prompt: Describe all transformations from x squared to negative two times x plus one squared, plus three.
solution_narration: Shift left one. Reflect the outputs across the horizontal axis and stretch their magnitudes by two.
Then shift up three. The vertex is negative one, three, and the parabola opens downward.

worked_examples.title: Three apples

labels: Three apples · one shared price p

narration: Three apples have the same price. Together they cost twelve dollars. Let p be the price of one apple.
There are exactly three apples in the diagram, so the total cost is three times p.
Divide both sides by three to isolate p. Each apple costs four dollars. Check by multiplying three by four.

worked_examples.title: Price plus delivery

labels: Four apples · delivery is a separate $2 fee

narration: Four equally priced apples plus a two dollar delivery fee cost eighteen dollars.
Remove the fee from both sides first: the apples themselves cost sixteen dollars.
Now divide by four to find the unit price. Each apple costs four dollars. The delivery fee is not an extra apple.

worked_examples.title: Cost graph
narration: A graph connects the number of apples to their total cost at four dollars each.
The horizontal coordinate counts apples; the vertical coordinate measures dollars. The points zero, zero and three, twelve lie on the graph.
The straight line represents the algebraic relationship. In this shopping context only whole-number apple counts describe actual purchases.

solution_narration: Subtract the fixed fee of 0 from the total. This leaves 6 dollars for 3 apples.
Divide by 3. The price of each apple is 2 dollars.
Subtract the fixed fee of 1 from the total. This leaves 12 dollars for 4 apples.
Divide by 4. The price of each apple is 3 dollars.
The two outside the brackets multiplies the whole quantity. Divide both sides by two first.
Then subtract three. The solution is six. Check: twice nine is eighteen.
Subtract two p from both sides so that one p remains on the left.
Subtract two to obtain p equals six. Substitution gives twenty on both sides.
The proposed step ignores the fixed fee. Remove the two before dividing the apple cost into four equal shares.
The correct price is four, not four and a half.
A two dollar fee is the vertical intercept. Subtract it from the total cost.
Fifteen dollars at three dollars per item buys five items. The algebraic intersection has a whole-number input, which fits the purchase context.
Subtract the fixed fee of 0 from the total. This leaves 6 dollars for 3 apples.
Divide by 3. The price of each apple is 2 dollars.

misconception.wrong_reasoning: Subtract three from twelve to find the unit price.
misconception.correction: Three is the number of equal groups. Divide twelve by three.

opening.title: Three apples. One unknown price.
narration: Three apples cost twelve dollars. What does one apple cost?
We will turn the objects into an equation and check the result.

labels: Three apples · one shared price p

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the model to the word problem

worked_examples.title: Build the rectangle
narration: One square x-squared tile, five x-tiles, and six unit tiles can form a rectangle.
Arrange two x-tiles on one edge and three on the other. The corner needs two times three unit tiles: exactly six.
The side lengths are x plus two and x plus three, so their product is the original polynomial. The tile picture assumes a positive length x; the algebraic identity holds for every real x.

worked_examples.title: Solve by factoring
narration: Now set the polynomial equal to zero. The factored form gives a product of two quantities.
A product is zero only when at least one factor is zero. Solve the two resulting linear equations separately.
The solutions are negative two and negative three. Negative roots are algebraic solutions, not negative physical tile lengths.

worked_examples.title: Check the intercepts
narration: For the second polynomial, find numbers whose product is negative six and whose sum is negative one. They are negative three and positive two.
The factors are x minus three and x plus two. Their zeros are three and negative two.
The graph meets the horizontal axis at these same inputs. Substituting either root into the original polynomial gives zero.

solution_narration: The factor constants must add to 3 and multiply to 2. Use 1 and 2.
Set each factor equal to zero. The roots are negative 1 and negative 2.
The factor constants must add to 6 and multiply to 8. Use 2 and 4.
Set each factor equal to zero. The roots are negative 2 and negative 4.
Choose factor constants with product negative six and sum negative one. They are negative three and positive two.
The zeros are three and negative two.
The leading coefficient is two, so one factor has two x. Multiply the factors to check the middle term negative seven x.
Set each factor equal to zero, obtaining one half and three.
The two cross products are both three x. Their sum is six x.
The middle term is missing from the proposed expansion.
Expand the area equation and move twenty to the left.
Factoring gives candidate values negative seven and two. The positive-length condition leaves x equal to two, with rectangle sides four and five.
The factor constants must add to 3 and multiply to 2. Use 1 and 2.
Set each factor equal to zero. The roots are negative 1 and negative 2.

misconception.correction: Each factor must equal zero, giving negative 2 and negative 3.

opening.title: Can these tiles make one rectangle?
narration: A polynomial can encode an area. Arrange the pieces and its factors become side lengths.
We will use that structure to solve equations and verify their roots on a graph.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the model to the word problem

worked_examples.title: Quarter turn
narration: A unit circle has radius one. Begin on the positive horizontal axis and turn counterclockwise by a quarter revolution.
The point reaches zero, one. Cosine is its horizontal coordinate and sine its vertical coordinate.
At pi over two, cosine is zero and sine is one. These are coordinates, not distances measured around the circumference.

worked_examples.title: Second quadrant
narration: Two pi over three lies in the second quadrant. Its reference angle is pi over three.
The horizontal coordinate is negative one half while the vertical coordinate is positive square root of three over two.
The signs follow the point location. The reference triangle determines the coordinate magnitudes.

worked_examples.title: Circle to wave
narration: Now plot the vertical coordinate against the angle. A full turn produces one complete sine wave.
The output starts at zero, reaches one after a quarter turn, returns to zero after a half turn, then reaches negative one.
This graph records a changing coordinate. The horizontal axis now measures angle in radians rather than a position on the circle.

solution_narration: At a quarter turn the point is zero, one. Read the vertical coordinate.
At a half turn the point is negative one, zero. Read the horizontal coordinate.
At three quarters of a turn the point lies at zero, negative one.
A full revolution returns the point to one, zero.
The thirty degree reference triangle gives a vertical coordinate of one half.
The point is in the second quadrant. Its reference angle is pi over four, giving negative square root of two over two horizontally.
At a quarter turn the point is zero, one. Read the vertical coordinate.

misconception.correction: Cosine is horizontal and sine is vertical.

opening.title: A rotating point writes a wave
narration: A circle and a wave look different, but one moving coordinate connects them.
Track the vertical coordinate while the radius turns.

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the model to the word problem

worked_examples.title: Secant slope
narration: Let position be time squared. Between time two and time three the position increases from four to nine.
The average rate is the change in position divided by the change in time, giving five.
The straight secant line passes through the two measured points. Its slope is an average over the interval, not the instantaneous rate at the start.

worked_examples.title: Limit of secants
narration: Move the second measurement toward time two. The difference quotient simplifies to four plus h for nonzero h.
As h approaches zero, the secant slopes approach four. That limit defines the derivative at two.
The tangent line has slope four. We take a limit rather than divide by zero.

worked_examples.title: Position to velocity
narration: For this second motion model, position is three time squared plus two time. Suppose position is in metres and time in seconds.
Differentiating gives six time plus two, measured in metres per second.
At time two the velocity is fourteen metres per second. The machine separates the time input in seconds from the velocity output in metres per second.

solution_narration: Apply the power rule: multiply by 2, then reduce the power to 1.
Evaluate at two to get 4. This is a rate at a point, not the function value.
Differentiate each term. The constant one contributes zero.
At x equal to two, six times four minus five gives nineteen.
Rewrite the reciprocal as x to the power negative one.
The power rule gives negative one times x to the negative two. At two the slope is negative one quarter.
The tangent line needs both a point and a slope. The point is three, nine and the derivative there is six.
Use point-slope form and simplify to y equals six x minus nine.
Assume position is in metres and time in seconds. Differentiate position to obtain velocity.
At two seconds the velocity is nine metres per second. The units describe a rate, not a distance.
A zero derivative only identifies a candidate stationary point.
For x cubed at zero the derivative vanishes, but the function keeps increasing through the point. There is no local maximum there.
Apply the power rule: multiply by 2, then reduce the power to 1.
Evaluate at two to get 4. This is a rate at a point, not the function value.

misconception.wrong_reasoning: Set h equal to zero before simplifying the difference quotient.
misconception.correction: Simplify for nonzero h and then take the limit.

opening.title: Average speed is not speed at an instant
narration: A car can cover an interval at an average speed while changing its speed throughout.
How can two nearby measurements tell us the rate at one instant?

supporting_representations.learning_goal: Connect the model to the word problem
